The other AI agents, and where Archie wins.

Ten agents, placed from what their own pages say. Archie works on your own computer, on an AI account you own, and asks first on the steps that matter: nothing is sent until you send it. Where one of the other nine does something better, this page says so.

Join the Waitlist See It Work →

Archie is in testing. The waitlist hears the day it opens. See where it stands →

Every price on these pages was read from the other company’s own pricing page, and dated. Each page carries its own Checked date, the most recent being August 24, 2026; a figure older than 90 days fails our own build check rather than sitting here quietly going stale.

Every assistant we could source

Ten assistants, placed from what their own pages say.

Privacy runs across: where the work happens, on their servers or on your computer. What runs up is your pick. Asks first is what a product does before a step that matters: it acts unless you set it to ask, it asks by default until you change a setting, or it asks every time and there is no setting. Ease is how you get it running: from a terminal, by downloading an app, or by signing in. Those two and privacy are what this site is built around, which is why the chart rests on them. The top right is the corner we are aiming at, and in the Ease view nobody has reached it, us included. Every mark is placed by a sentence on the company’s own site, quoted below. Read September 18, 2026.

Where Archie wins

The work happens on your computer, on an AI account you own

Your files, your conversations and your sign-ins stay on a computer you already have, and your words go straight to the AI company you picked, from a choice of 7, on your own account. Five of the other nine say the work happens on a computer their company runs, and Wix publishes no program for your computer at all. The three that run on yours are named below. Archie will also run on a model on your own computer instead of an account anywhere: it looks for Ollama, LM Studio or llama.cpp, then hands the model a tool and checks it can use one before binding it, because plenty of small models cannot. Vellum and OpenClaw offer that too.

The asking has no off switch

Calendar changes are confirmed, nothing is sent until you send it, and it stops before an order is final. On Archie none of that is a setting. Every other agent on the board that asks can be told to stop asking, and three of them act on their own by defaultSource 5.

The AI is billed at cost, with a cap you set

$30 a month for the app, and the AI on your own account at the AI company’s own price, with a spending cap you set thereSource 2. The rented agents sell a tier, and the tier is the meter.

If we stop, you keep Archie

Our Terms commit us to a final build that needs no sign-inSource 1. A rented agent lasts as long as the rental does.

Where the other nine beat Archie

Hermes, OpenClaw and Vellum run on your own computer, cost nothing to keep and are open source, and if free and open is how you are choosing, they win it. Their code is published and ours is not, so anything you can imagine you can write, and you can read every line before you trust it. That is the larger freedom if you are the person who would use it, and the chart does not draw it, because the chart measures what happens without writing code. All three let you pick the AI company, as Archie does. OpenClaw gives you the most control of the ten: five permission modes, one of which asks before every command, allow lists per command, and code you can read and change. Vellum has a Strict mode that asks before everything, and Hermes can be set to ask more or less. On Archie the asking is built in and has no setting, which is the trade the chart draws: less to set up, and less you can change. Vellum makes almost the same custody claim we do, in almost the same words, and reaches a phone, a browser and a terminal besides. Muse and Symphony each have a free plan that renews every month, and ours does not.

What you can change, and what you cannot

Not on the chart, because it did not separate anybody. Six of the other nine will also write you a new ability if you ask them for one, so this is where Archie stands rather than where it wins.

Describe a skill and your agent writes it

Say what you wish it could do, in your own words. It asks a couple of questions, writes the skill, and comes back with a card naming what it assumed. Press Keep it and your agent has it. The Skills tab carries the form if you would rather fill the fields in yourself, and specialists and routines are written the same two ways.

Add your own instructions to anything on the shelf

Every add-on takes extra instructions from you, and an update leaves them alone. A personality sets the voice. Eight switches decide what your agent may do at all, and turning one off also makes every message cost a little less.

A new ability has to come from us

A skill is instructions plus permission to use something Archie already has. Which services and which abilities exist is decided when we build the app, so a new one is a new version and we are the only ones who can release it. On Hermes, OpenClaw and Vellum you would write it yourself, because their code is published.

Archie’s code is not published

You can watch every connection it makes with a network monitor, and our proof page hands you the commands. You cannot read the source, and we are not going to pretend that is the same thing.

What a drawing leaves out

No drawing shows the distance between installing something and having it do your actual job: the accounts wired up, the rules that match how you work, and somebody to ask when it breaks. That gap is what the six comparisons below are about, and it is the honest place to argue with an agent you could run yourself for nothing.

Sources for every mark above
1Archie: custody and what it asks

Our own Trust page, claim by claim, with the code behind each one. Archie is a download from our install page, which is the app row. Its shelf is the add-ons page, which is the shelf; Archie’s own code is not published. Telling your agent what you wish it did, and having it write the skill, shipped in Archie 0.2.2 on September 1, 2026.

2Archie: the price

Our own pricing page.

3Vellum: runs locally by default, and asks until you mark an action trusted

Read from vellum.ai on September 16, 2026. “By default, your assistant runs locally. Your conversation history, memory, and credentials stay on your machine and are never used to train models.” And: “High-stakes actions like sending emails to new contacts, modifying important files, or spending credits require explicit approval until you mark them as trusted.” Its download page, read September 18, offers “Vellum for Mac: Native Mac app with computer use” and “Vellum for Windows: Desktop app for Windows PCs”, which is the app row. Its permissions docs give four modes, from Strict, “Everything: every action requires explicit approval”, to Full access, “your assistant never asks for permission”. Its FAQ says “you can switch between models including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, or open weights via Ollama at any time.” The page also says Vellum is open source and is “native to Mac and accessible everywhere: iOS, Android, web app, voice, email, Telegram, Slack, and terminal.” Its skills page, read September 18, says “Skills give your agents new capabilities. Browse the catalog, pick what you need, and install with a single command”, and its plugins page says to “Browse and install from the Plugins tab inside the Vellum app”; with the code open, its code is yours to change. Its docs, read September 18, also say “You can create new skills by describing what you want in the chat”, and that the agent “writes the instructions” itself.

4Vellum: free to start, then $30, $100 or $200 a month

Read from vellum.ai/pricing on September 16, 2026. “Vellum is free to download and start.” The paid plans are Mighty at $30, Super at $100 and Ultra at $200 a month, each described as a computer of a given size; Mighty is a “Small computer 1 vCPU / 2 GiB, 10 GB storage”. Usage beyond a plan is metered in credits at “$1 = 1 credit”. We do not say where a paid Vellum plan executes, because Vellum does not say.

5OpenClaw: on your machine, free, and acting on its own by default

Read from openclaw.ai on September 16, 2026. “Mac, Windows, or Linux. Bring hosted, subscription-backed, gateway, or local models. State lives on your machine, not a vendor cloud.” And: “No subscription. No hosted tier. No token.” OpenClaw “is stewarded by the OpenClaw Foundation, an independent US 501(c)(3) non-profit” and is MIT licensed. It reaches “WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal, iMessage, or any of its 29 channels.” Its docs, read the same day, place it: on tool and agent permissions, “Full Access, including Default (Full Access), authorizes permitted changes without an approval prompt; restricted runs require human approval”, and on exec approvals, “Commands run only when policy + allowlist + (optional) user approval all agree.” So by default it acts on its own, and you can make it ask. Read again September 18: its docs give five exec modes, “deny”, “allowlist”, “ask”, “auto” and “full”, an “ask: always” that “keeps prompting”, and per-command allow lists, which is the most control on this board. Its getting-started is a shell command, “Try it in one command”, and changing its permissions is another, openclaw config set tools.exec.mode, which is the terminal row; openclaw.ai also offers “Desktop Apps: Full apps that install everything for you”, and both are true. The same page lists “Skills & Plugins: Extend with community skills or build your own” and “ClawHub: Install skills and plugins”, and with MIT code its code is yours to change. Its Skill Workshop docs, read September 18, say “ask the agent for the skill you want” and give the example “Make a skill called morning-catchup that runs my Monday inbox routine.”

6Hermes: desktop or cloud, free and MIT, and asking by default

Read from hermes-agent.nousresearch.com on September 16, 2026, the Nous Research page for it. It offers a desktop app for macOS 12+, Windows 10/11 and Linux, and “Deploy to the cloud” through Nous Portal. It is “free and open source under the MIT license”, and Nous Portal plans run from $0 to $200 a month for credits and hosted services. It reaches “Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Email, CLI”. Its security docs, read the same day, do: “Before executing any command, Hermes checks it against a curated list of dangerous patterns. If a match is found, the user must explicitly approve it”, with three modes, “smart | manual | off”. Its README says “Use any model you want”, naming Nous Portal, OpenRouter, OpenAI and your own endpoint. Its site leads with “Download desktop app”, then “Deploy to the cloud”, then “Install via terminal”, and its FAQ says “Download Hermes Desktop for macOS or Windows, or use the terminal installation command above”, which is the app row; Linux is terminal only. Its skills docs, read September 18, say “Browse, search, install, and manage skills from online registries, skills.sh, direct well-known skill endpoints, and official optional skills”, and with MIT code its code is yours to change. The same docs add /learn, “the fast way to turn something you already know … into a reusable skill, without hand-writing the SKILL.md”.

7Claude Cowork: Anthropic’s servers, and a mode that does not ask

Read from Anthropic’s own Cowork guide on August 20, 2026. “Open Claude on the web at claude.ai, in the Claude Desktop app, or in the Claude mobile app”, choose Cowork, and “describe the task you want Claude to complete”, which is the sign-in row. Cowork’s work “runs on Anthropic’s servers, in an isolated environment, and your sessions and files are saved to your Claude account”. It has three permission modes; in Skip mode “Claude doesn’t pause to ask and nothing checks its actions automatically”. Re-read September 16, 2026: the mode selector “offers Auto and Manual (default)”, and in Manual, “formerly ‘Ask before acting’”, “Claude pauses and asks for approval for actions.” Its overview, read September 18, says “You manage connectors, skills, and plugins from Customize in the sidebar”, and its skills guide says “In Cowork, click Customize in the left sidebar, then click the ‘+’ button to open the directory”, so ready-made abilities can be added to it, as they can to Archie. Anthropic’s skills page, read September 18, also offers a skill-creator: “Describe what you want, and Claude generates the folder structure, formats the SKILL.md file, and bundles your resources.”

8Claude Cowork: included from Pro up, $20 a month

Read from claude.com/pricing on August 19 and 20, 2026: “Includes Claude Cowork” on the Pro card, and Pro at $20 a month, or $17 a month billed annually.

9Grok Bot: a persistent cloud VM

Read from x.ai/news/introducing-grok-bot and the Grok Bot overview on August 20, 2026. Each Grok Bot “runs on a persistent cloud VM with a browser, filesystem, and terminal” and signs in to your tools there; it comes back “when something needs your approval”. Re-read September 16, 2026: “They finish jobs end to end, and only come back when something needs your approval”, and “Bots share a computer of their own in the cloud”. The same page says “Download the app, create your first teammate, and start handing off work”, with a Download for macOS button, which is the app row. Its marketplace, read in a browser on September 18, lists bots by category with an Add button on each, so ready-made abilities can be added to it, as they can to Archie. Its docs, read September 18, also write a skill on request: “Save the process we just used as a skill called ‘Weekly account health’”, and you can “set its name, label, description, and avatar”.

10Grok Bot: which plans carry it

Plan cards read in a browser at x.ai/bot on August 20, 2026, because x.ai refuses automated requests: SuperGrok Heavy at $300 a month and Cursor Ultra at $200 a month, with Cursor Teams Premium at $120 a seat also carrying it. No script of ours can re-confirm this one, so it is re-read by hand.

11Meta Muse: a dedicated cloud computer, free for most

Read from Meta’s own announcement on September 15, 2026. Muse “runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else’s agent can reach it”, and is “free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more”. It is “rolling out in the US on iOS, Android, and muse.ai” and “Anyone can use it out of the box, no technical experience required”, which is the sign-in row. Its permissions are one of two settings: “Always ask”, before any action, or “Ask for some actions”. The announcement says “People choose which apps Muse connects to and exactly how much access it gets”, and Meta’s help centre, read September 18, says “You can choose to connect Muse to apps and services provided by Meta or third-parties. We call these Connectors.” Meta publishes no shelf of add-ons, and its help centre says “Skills are developed by Meta and are already part of Muse”, so on that page what a person changes is settings, connectors, and the name, personality and tone, which Meta says you can alter by asking in the conversation. Meta’s own engineering blog goes further, saying Muse “builds its own tools” and “can also write its own custom connectors”. The two Meta pages disagree and we are not going to pick a winner for them.

12Meta Muse: what it will not do without approval

Read from Meta’s help centre on September 15, 2026: “By default, Muse will not take many important actions, like sending an email, without your approval.”

13Wix Symphony: how you reach it, and where the work happens

Read from wix.com/symphony on September 11, 2026. Symphony is used with a Wix account, in a browser or its iOS and Android apps, and Wix publishes no program you run on your own computer, which is the sign-in row. Read again September 18: Wix’s own overview says “Your agents connect to the suite of tools you already use and can work on their own, 24/7, to help grow your business and manage day-to-day tasks”, and that “your agents’ background work uses AI credits”. Wix publishes no sentence saying where that work runs. Work that goes on while you are away, on a product that ships only a phone app and a browser, is not happening on a computer of yours, and that is why Symphony sits on the their-servers side: it is our reading of those two sentences, not a quote, and if Wix publishes the sentence either way we will cite it. The same overview says Symphony “integrates with your existing tools and workflows, like your calendars, email inbox, productivity tools, Slack, Salesforce, and much more”, and the product page says “Create and train your own agent. Set its name, give it a personality, approve goals and actions”; no shelf of add-ons is published, so what a person can change is settings and the accounts they connect.

14Wix Symphony: it checks first

Read from Wix’s own overview on September 11, 2026: Symphony “checks with you first before your agents act, so nothing important happens without your approval”.

15Wix Symphony: the plans

Read from wix.com/symphony/pricing on September 11, 2026: a free plan with no credit card needed, then Basic at $16 a month, Pro at $40 and Max at $80, cheaper billed annually. The free plan’s daily credit cap was 50 when we first read this page in August and is 100 now, which is worth knowing against anything written earlier, ours included.

16Instinct: in private access, hosted, and acting on its own

Read from instinct.com on September 16, 2026. “Instinct is a personal assistant that understands what you’re working on and what’s important to you.” It “connects to your applications and devices - email, messaging, screen, audio, location, and more”, and “It’s trained to use a phone and a computer. You can text or call it.” It is “currently available to a private access group as we’re scaling up compute”. “Text Instinct to get started”: nothing is installed, which is the sign-in row. The page gives no price. Its privacy policy, read the same day, places it: the service is provided with “third-party hosting”, its features “can perform tasks or take actions independently on your behalf, based on the permissions you grant”, and it uses “third-party AI model providers who help support the Services”. Nothing on its page is installed beyond what it connects to, so what a person can change is settings and the accounts they connect. Other companies have written about what Instinct does; we do not print those claims, because a competitor writing about a competitor is not a source.

17Norton Family Assistant: asks first, runs in the cloud, and prices nothing

Read from us.norton.com/products/family-assistant on September 16, 2026. It “keeps your family organized, so you never miss to-dos, calendar events, and important updates in your life”, “Plugs into the apps your family already uses”, and “Asks first, acts after”; its FAQ adds “Every send, payment and booking waits for your approval” and that “the AI providers we use operate under enterprise contracts with zero data retention”. Norton says “Your chats are never shared, sold or used to train AI.” The product page carries no price. Its support FAQ, read September 18, 2026, says where it runs: “Family Assistant runs a per-user instance architecture: your family graph, connected-account tokens, agent context, and chat history all live inside your own dedicated instance in the cloud, isolated from other users”, which is why it sits on the their-servers side. It “works on any PCs that run in browsers such as Norton Neo, Chrome, and Firefox” or as an iPhone app, which is the sign-in row, and it “can connect to accounts and services you choose”, with no shelf of add-ons published, so what a person can change is settings and the accounts they connect.

How these are written

Every page says where the other option wins.

A comparison with no losses in it is an advertisement, and you would be right to read it as one. So each of these carries a section naming what the alternative does better, every price is read from that company’s own pricing page and dated on the page, and every figure links to where it was read so you can check it yourself.
